subsection: 3. The Irish countryside, economic crisis and the Great Famine: causes, course and government responses, 1815–1850

notes.b: Land was held through a chain of tenure, and the mass of the population depended on the potato and on small plots of land.
points: Landlords held the estates, and many were absentees who lived in England or on the Continent and left their estates to agents.
Middlemen, also called head tenants, leased large holdings from landlords and sublet them to smaller tenants at a profit.
Strong farmers held substantial holdings of land and were the most prosperous tenants in the countryside.
Cottiers held a small cabin and a plot of land in return for labour on the farm, and labourers had no land at all.
Conacre was the letting of land for a single season, usually for potatoes, and it was the main way the poorest families obtained a food supply.
Population grew rapidly between 1791 and 1841, and subdivision of holdings increased dependence on the potato as the main food crop.

notes.b: Agricultural prices collapsed after the end of the French Wars in 1815, and the rural economy stagnated for the next thirty years.
points: Grain prices fell sharply after the end of the Napoleonic Wars in 1815, and farmers who had expanded tillage during the wars faced ruin.
The decline of rural industry, especially hand-loom weaving, removed a source of supplementary income for many families.
Partial famines occurred in 1816–1817, 1822 and 1830–1831, when harvest failure forced many families to depend on relief.
The Devon Commission, which sat from 1843 to 1845, investigated the land system and found widespread insecurity of tenure and poverty.
Rent arrears and evictions increased in the 1830s and early 1840s, as tenants with small holdings could not pay their rent after bad harvests.

notes.h: The blight and the Famine's course, 1845–1850
notes.b: The potato blight destroyed the crop in successive years, and mass hunger, disease and emigration followed.
points: Potato blight, caused by the fungus Phytophthora infestans, first appeared in Ireland in September 1845, destroying much of that year's crop.
In 1846 the blight returned more widely and destroyed most of the crop, and the Famine became a national disaster.
The period 1846–1847, known as Black '47, was the worst year for hunger, with mass starvation in the west and south-west.
Fever, particularly typhus and relapsing fever, spread through the population weakened by hunger and was a leading cause of death.
Regional variation was marked: the west and south-west, including Connacht and Munster, suffered the worst losses, while Ulster and parts of the east were less severely affected.
Population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.5 million in 1851 through death and emigration, a fall of roughly one-fifth in a decade (about).

notes.b: Peel's Conservative government tried to meet the crisis through the purchase and sale of Indian corn and public works.
points: Peel's government set up a Relief Commission in 1845 under Commissary-General Sir John Routh, and it arranged the import of Indian corn to be sold at low prices.
The Indian meal was sold through local shops and relief depots, and it was unpopular because of its coarse texture and unfamiliar taste.
The Board of Works was given responsibility for public works schemes, which employed labourers on roads and other projects.
Peel's government repealed the Corn Laws in 1846, which opened British markets to cheap imported grain, but the repeal came too late to prevent the Famine.
The government's aim was to avoid direct charitable provision and to keep relief temporary, a principle that it applied to its public works schemes.

notes.b: The Whig government under Lord John Russell replaced Peel's measures with a system based on local relief and the principle of laissez-faire.
points: Russell's Whig government took office in June 1846 and was committed to laissez-faire, the principle that the government should not interfere with the operation of the market.
The Indian meal depots were closed in 1847, and the government left food supply to private traders, who failed to meet the demand.
The public works schemes were ended in favour of direct local relief, which was paid out by the poor law system and was supposed to be funded by local ratepayers.
The Temporary Relief Act of 1847 introduced soup kitchens, which gave cooked food to the destitute, and at their peak they fed about three million people (about).
Charles Trevelyan, Assistant Secretary to the Treasury, managed the government's relief expenditure and argued that the Famine was a mechanism for removing a surplus population.

notes.b: Trevelyan was the senior British civil servant responsible for relief policy in 1846–1847, and his views on the Famine remain controversial.
points: Charles Edward Trevelyan was born in 1807 and entered the civil service, rising to the post of Assistant Secretary to the Treasury, where he was in charge of Irish relief from 1845.
He was a participant in the government's relief policy, and he controlled the expenditure and the decision to close the public works schemes.
He believed that the Famine was a providential event that would correct the Irish economy by removing excess population and sweeping away the old system of land tenure.
His book The Irish Crisis, published in 1848, presented the Famine as a judgement on the Irish people and defended the government's policy of limited relief.
Contemporaries were divided: supporters praised his efficiency and his commitment to economy, while critics such as Irish nationalists and many relief workers blamed his policy for mass starvation.
Later historians have judged his role as central to the failure of relief, and they have pointed to the influence of laissez-faire and the belief that charity demoralised the poor.

notes.h: Legislation and the post-Famine land system, 1847–1850
notes.b: The Poor Law Extension Act and the rate-in-aid shifted the cost of relief onto property owners, and the land system was altered by evictions and new laws.
points: The Poor Law Extension Act of 1847 extended poor law relief to the able-bodied poor and made property owners liable for the poor rate on the whole of their holdings.
The Gregory clause, named after the MP William Gregory, denied relief to any tenant who held more than a quarter acre of land, which led to the surrender of holdings and to evictions.
The rate-in-aid of 1849 was a special tax levied on the richer poor law unions to support the poorest, and it was intended to share the cost across Ireland.
The Encumbered Estates Act of 1849 allowed the sale of indebted estates through a court, which brought new landowners into the countryside.
Evictions were carried out on a large scale during and after the Famine, and the number of families evicted rose sharply between 1847 and 1849.

notes.h: Food exports and the government's record
notes.b: Irish food continued to be exported during the Famine, and critics then and later used this to question the government's priorities.
points: Grain, cattle and other food continued to be exported from Irish ports during the Famine, a fact that critics used to show that food was available but was not distributed to those in need.
Relief was most effective where local committees were active, and it was least effective in the west, where poor law unions lacked funds.
Historians have debated whether the government could have prevented the Famine's mortality; many now argue that its reliance on local ratepayers and the market was the main cause of excess deaths.
The Famine is generally judged to have caused about one million deaths from starvation and disease, and about one million emigrants left the country in the same years (about).

keyTerms.definition: The system in which large landowners held estates let to tenants, often through middlemen, and the tenants' security depended on the landlord's decisions.
The fall in agricultural prices after 1815, the decline of rural industry and the periodic harvest failures which left the rural population poor.

The mass starvation and disease that followed the potato blight of 1845–1849, which caused about one million deaths and large-scale emigration.
